text.title: Audience Segmentation Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules that separate a segmentation from a persona deck: executable assignment rules over observable fields, a behavioural basis, per-number sourcing on the six-criterion attractiveness score, bottom-up sizing, a named reachable channel, and one primary target with the runner-up named.

rule.statement: Every segment definition MUST carry an assignment rule expressed over fields that exist in a real record store (CRM, analytics, onboarding form) and can be run as a query — e.g. "plan_tier IN (pro, geek) AND sessions_last_28d >= 8 AND seats = 1". Run against the full customer/prospect table, each record MUST land in exactly one segment and the unassignable residue MUST be <= 5% and reported. A definition that cannot be executed against a record is a persona, not a segment.

rationale.source: Minto Pyramid Principle (MECE) + operational CRM segmentation practice

rule.rationale: Overlapping definitions double-count the same account in two segment sizes, so the sizing model inflates and campaign attribution becomes ambiguous — the same user is "primary" in two plans. A definition with no assignment rule can never be applied to an actual list, so the artefact terminates as a slide instead of a targeting filter.

rule.statement: At least one of the 2-3 dimensions MUST be behavioural (observed usage, purchase trigger, frequency, channel) or needs/job-based. A dimension set consisting only of demographic or firmographic descriptors (age, company size, geography, industry) is rejected.
rule.rationale: Demographics are proxies for the thing that actually drives choice. Two accounts identical on size and industry can be hiring the product for opposite jobs and respond to opposite messages, so a purely demographic split leaves within-segment variance roughly equal to the population's — the split buys no predictive power and every segment gets the same campaign.

rule.statement: Each segment MUST be scored on all six attractiveness criteria (size, growth, willingness-to-pay, reachability cost, competitive intensity, capability fit) on one declared scale, and every individual cell MUST carry a source reference. A cell with no source is emitted as null and excluded from the composite, never filled with an estimate.

rationale.source: GE-McKinsey market-attractiveness matrix; Kotler & Keller MSADA criteria

rule.rationale: A weighted composite launders its inputs: once six guesses are averaged into "72", the number is quoted downstream with no way to see that five of the six were opinions. Nulling unsourced cells makes the composite's coverage visible and points at exactly which number is worth going out to measure.

rule.statement: Segment size MUST be computed bottom-up as a stated denominator times a qualification rate times a reachable share, with a source for each factor (e.g. registry count, survey incidence, ad-platform audience estimate). "N% of a TAM figure" and any size stated without its factors is rejected.

rationale.source: Bottom-up market sizing practice in investor diligence

rule.rationale: A top-down percentage has no falsifiable input, so it can never be shown wrong and never be improved — it survives every review unchanged. Bottom-up decomposition puts each assumption on its own line, so a reviewer can attack the qualification rate specifically and the number moves when new evidence arrives.

rule.statement: Each segment MUST name at least one concrete channel where its members are addressable — a specific ad-platform targeting spec, a named list/community/event, or an owned-data segment — plus an observed or benchmark cost per qualified contact. "Online", "social" and a bare platform name with no targeting spec fail this rule.

rationale.source: Kotler & Keller — the Accessible criterion of effective segmentation

rule.rationale: A segment that is definable but not addressable produces zero pipeline at any budget, and the failure surfaces months later as "the campaign underperformed" rather than "the segment was never reachable". Forcing a channel plus a unit cost at definition time makes the reachability constraint fail fast and feeds CAC directly into the attractiveness score.

rule.statement: Exactly one target_segment is selected. The rationale MUST name the runner-up segment and the specific criterion on which it lost, with both scores. "We will serve both" and unranked ties are rejected.
rule.rationale: Two primaries split the roadmap and the messaging, and the product ends up second-best for both. Recording the deciding criterion and the two scores turns the choice into a re-checkable claim: when that one number is re-measured and flips, the reversal is mechanical instead of a fresh six-week debate.

rule.statement: Do NOT run this methodology when (a) there is no record store with per-user behavioural fields to execute assignment rules against — run persona-building or JTBD interviews first, (b) the product is pre-launch with no customers and no interview corpus, so every segment score would be unsourced, (c) the behavioural data available is older than ~18 months or covers only retained customers, since churned and never-converted records are the segments you most need to see.

rationale.source: Methodology preconditions — survivorship bias in customer-only datasets

rule.rationale: Segmenting a retained-customers-only table describes the people who already fit, so the output recommends targeting the segment you already own and is read as validation. Without assignable fields the exercise degrades into persona writing under a segmentation label, which is worse than an honest skip because downstream teams treat it as targetable.
